description: Compare Google Docs voice typing and Wispr Flow for Mac users. Learn which tool fits your workflow for dictation, privacy, and system-wide support.
targetKeyword: google docs voice typing vs wispr flow
intro: Choosing between Google Docs voice typing and Wispr Flow depends on where you need to dictate. Google Docs voice typing is a free, browser-based tool built specifically for Google's ecosystem, while Wispr Flow is a dedicated Mac application designed to work across every app on your system.
tldr: Google Docs voice typing is free but restricted to Google's web-based editors.
Wispr Flow works system-wide in any Mac app but requires a paid subscription for full features.
Lazur offers a third path, acting as a voice assistant that sees your screen and helps you work, alongside high-quality dictation.
Privacy-conscious users should weigh cloud-only processing against local memory and security needs.

blocks.text: Google Docs voice typing: The basics

Google Docs voice typing is a free tool found inside the Tools menu of any Google Doc. It is simple to use. Open a document, go to Tools > Voice typing, and click the microphone icon. It supports about 120 languages and accents. You can use basic voice commands to format text, but only if your account and document language are set to English.

The main limitation is its environment. It lives only in your web browser. If you switch to Apple Mail, Slack, or a local text editor like Obsidian, the feature stops working. You must also keep a stable internet connection because all audio processing happens on Google's servers.

Wispr Flow is an application you install on your Mac. It is built to function across every app you use. You can dictate into your browser, your code editor, or your email client. It handles messy speech well, automatically removing filler words and applying grammar corrections in real-time.

The app includes features like a customizable dictionary and snippets. It also has a specific mode for voice-based editing. While it offers a free plan, it limits you to 2,000 words per week. For heavy users, the Pro and Growth plans offer more capacity.

When you look at Google Docs voice typing vs Wispr Flow, consider your privacy needs. Google processes audio in the cloud and may retain recordings to improve its models. Wispr Flow also processes in the cloud but provides clearer options to opt out of training. Both apps require an active internet connection for transcription.

blocks.caption: Comparison of voice tools for Mac users.

blocks.text: Lazur is a different kind of tool. It lives in your Mac notch and acts as a voice assistant that can see your screen. If you hold ⌥ ⌘, you can ask questions about anything visible. Lazur answers out loud. If you ask how to perform a task, it draws a circle around the button you need to click and guides you one step at a time.

If you just need to dictate text, hold the fn key. Lazur provides clean, formatted dictation in any application. It includes clipboard slots and a personal dictionary. Unlike tools that only type for you, Lazur remembers what you asked and helps you manage your Mac workflow without requiring you to switch between different apps.

faq.question: Does Google Docs voice typing work in other apps?
faq.answer: No, it is strictly limited to Google Docs and Google Slides within a supported web browser.

faq.question: Can I use Wispr Flow offline?
faq.answer: No, Wispr Flow requires an active internet connection for its cloud-based transcription.

faq.question: How does Lazur differ from dictation-only apps?
faq.answer: Lazur is a voice assistant that sees your screen and guides you through tasks, in addition to providing system-wide dictation.

verdict: If you live entirely in Google Docs, the built-in voice typing is a fine, free choice. If you need to dictate in Slack, email, or other desktop apps, Wispr Flow is a strong option. For those who want more than just dictation, Lazur offers a unique assistant that can see your screen and guide you through complex tasks on your Mac.
